title: Trump Halts New Russia Sanctions, Citing Waiver as U.S. National Interest – AP News
body:
President Donald Trump signed an executive order on Friday that temporarily suspends a sweeping sanctions package aimed at crippling Russia’s economy, arguing that a short‑term waiver serves the United States’ national interest. The move halts the legislation, known as the Lindsey Graham‑named “Russia Sanctions Act,” which had been passed by Congress earlier this year and was set to impose unprecedented restrictions on Russian banks, energy firms, and key export sectors.

The executive order, issued under the president’s authority to grant waivers for national security reasons, pauses the enforcement of the sanctions for an initial period of 90 days. In a brief statement, the White House said the decision allows the administration to “assess the broader implications for American businesses, energy security, and geopolitical stability.” The pause does not cancel the legislation; rather, it delays its implementation while the administration conducts a review and seeks input from relevant agencies and industry stakeholders.

Congressional leaders expressed sharp disappointment, accusing the president of undermining a bipartisan effort to hold Moscow accountable for its ongoing aggression in Ukraine and its alleged interference in U.S. elections. Senate Majority Leader Chuck Schumer called the waiver “a reckless gamble that rewards a rogue regime,” while House Foreign Affairs Committee Chairman Michael McCaul warned that the delay could erode the credibility of U.S. sanctions policy. Democrats, who had largely supported the bill, argued that the executive order signals a willingness to prioritize short‑term commercial concerns over long‑term security objectives.

The sanctions package itself was one of the most comprehensive measures ever proposed against Russia. It targeted the country’s sovereign wealth fund, restricted access to the U.S. dollar clearing system for major Russian banks, and barred American firms from exporting high‑technology components used in weapons and energy production. Proponents said the sanctions would choke off the financial lifelines that enable Moscow to fund its war effort, while critics warned they could also ripple through global markets, raising energy prices and disrupting supply chains for critical minerals.

Analysts note that the president’s decision reflects a broader tension within the administration between a hard‑line stance on foreign adversaries and the desire to protect domestic economic interests. Energy experts point out that the sanctions could have inadvertently strained U.S. energy firms that rely on Russian crude and gas imports, especially as the world grapples with volatile oil markets. Moreover, technology companies have raised concerns about compliance costs and the risk of losing access to Russian talent and research collaborations. By invoking a national‑interest waiver, the administration signals a willingness to balance these competing pressures, but it also raises questions about the predictability of U.S. policy for allies and partners.

Internationally, the pause has been met with cautious optimism by some European leaders who fear that an abrupt, all‑out sanctions regime could destabilize already fragile economies in the region. The European Union, which has coordinated its own sanctions with Washington, indicated that it will monitor the U.S. decision closely and adjust its own measures accordingly. Russia, for its part, hailed the move as a “victory for diplomacy” and pledged to continue its strategic partnerships with non‑Western nations, while also using the respite to seek ways to circumvent existing restrictions.

The next 90 days will be crucial in determining whether the waiver becomes a temporary measure or a stepping stone toward a more permanent recalibration of U.S. policy toward Russia. The administration has promised a detailed report to Congress before the waiver expires, outlining its findings on economic impact, national security considerations, and potential alternatives to the original sanctions framework. As the deadline approaches, lawmakers on both sides of the aisle are likely to intensify scrutiny, and the outcome may shape the future of American sanctions strategy in an increasingly multipolar world.
